question: What first made you want to study music seriously?
lookingFor: A genuine, specific origin story for their commitment to music, not a vague love of listening.

bullets: Name a specific moment, teacher, or piece that sparked it
Show how that moment turned into sustained commitment
Connect it to why they want to keep studying it now
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I started piano at six because my grandmother had one in her living room, but the real turning point was hearing my school orchestra play Dvorak's New World Symphony when I was twelve. I remember being unable to sit still, and I went home and learned the whole slow movement by ear on the piano. From there I started taking lessons more seriously, entered competitions, and now I can't imagine a version of my life where music isn't at the center of it.

commonMistakes: Saying 'I've just always loved music' with no specific memory
Describing only passive listening with no active commitment
Rushing past the story to talk about achievements instead
followUps: How has that early motivation changed since then?

question: Why do you want to study music at this university rather than go straight to a conservatoire or another course?
lookingFor: Specific understanding of what this program offers versus alternatives, showing genuine research.

bullets: Name a specific strength of the program, such as faculty, ensembles, or a dual academic-performance track
Explain why that fits their own goals better than a pure conservatoire route
Show they understand the difference between an academic music degree and conservatoire training
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I looked seriously at conservatoires, but I want to keep composing and studying music history alongside performance, not train purely as a performer. Your program lets me take analysis and ethnomusicology modules while still playing in the chamber ensembles, and I read that Dr. Okafor's seminar on twentieth century British music runs alongside the performance stream, which is exactly the mix I want. I don't just want to get better at my instrument, I want to understand the wider context I'm playing in.

commonMistakes: Generic praise that would apply to any music program
Not knowing the difference between conservatoire and university music study
No specific faculty, module, or ensemble mentioned
followUps: What would you do if the program pushed you more toward theory than performance?

question: Tell us about a piece of music that has had a big impact on you, and why.
lookingFor: Genuine, specific engagement with a piece, not just a title-drop.

bullets: Name a specific piece and what about it struck them
Describe what they noticed musically, such as harmony, structure, or texture, not only emotion
Connect it to their own development as a musician
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It's Shostakovich's Eighth String Quartet. I first heard it at fifteen and didn't understand why four instruments could sound so bleak, so I started pulling apart the score and realized how much of the effect comes from the DSCH motif repeating in different guises across all five movements. It changed how I listen to everything else, because now I'm always asking what small idea a whole piece is built from. It's part of why I got interested in analysis, not just performance.

commonMistakes: Naming a piece with no real detail about why it matters
Only an emotional reaction with no musical observation
Picking something to sound impressive rather than something genuine
followUps: Has your relationship with that piece changed as you've grown as a musician?

question: Tell us about your instrument and your training so far.
lookingFor: A clear, honest account of their musical background and level, without exaggeration.

bullets: State the instrument, how long they've studied, and current level or grade
Mention teachers, ensembles, or exams that shaped their development
Be honest about strengths and areas still developing
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've played cello for nine years and reached grade eight two years ago, and I've spent the time since working on repertoire rather than more exams, mostly Bach suites and the Elgar concerto. I studied with the same teacher for six years, who pushed me hard on tone production, and I play in a youth orchestra and a string quartet outside school. My sight-reading is still the weakest part of my playing, which is something I'm actively working on.

commonMistakes: Vague claims about ability with no concrete detail
Only listing grades with no sense of musicianship
Overstating ability in a way that won't survive a follow-up question
followUps: What repertoire are you working on right now?

question: Which composer do you feel closest to, and why?
lookingFor: A specific, informed connection to a composer's work beyond just naming a famous name.

bullets: Name a composer and specific works, not just a reputation
Explain what about their musical language or output resonates
Show awareness of the composer in historical or stylistic context
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Ravel, mostly because of how precise his orchestration is. I studied the score of Le Tombeau de Couperin and was amazed at how sparse the writing is compared to how full it sounds, every note is doing work. I like that he's often placed next to Debussy as an impressionist but his music is actually much more classically structured underneath, which is part of what draws me in. I keep coming back to him when I want to understand restraint in composition.

commonMistakes: Naming a composer with no specific works or reasons
Choosing someone purely because they sound impressive
Getting basic facts about the composer wrong
followUps: Is there a piece by them you'd love to perform but haven't yet?

subtopic: Practice and balancing technique with musicality
question: How do you structure your practice, and how do you avoid it becoming purely mechanical?
lookingFor: A thoughtful, disciplined approach to practice that treats musicality as inseparable from technique.

bullets: Describe a real structure, such as warm-up, technical work, then repertoire with slow practice
Show awareness of the difference between mechanical repetition and musical intent
Give a concrete example of catching themselves practicing badly and correcting it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I usually start with scales and etudes for about twenty minutes, then move to slow, detailed work on whatever passage is giving me trouble before I ever play a piece through at speed. I try to never run a passage more than a few times without asking what I actually want it to sound like, because I've noticed that mindless repetition just grooves in the same mistakes. Recently I caught myself practicing a Chopin nocturne so mechanically that it had gone flat emotionally, so I forced myself to sing the phrase out loud first to remember what I was actually going for.

commonMistakes: A vague answer with no real structure
Treating technique and musicality as unrelated
No self-awareness about when practice goes wrong
followUps: How do you know when a passage is actually ready?

question: Can you explain the difference between a perfect cadence and an imperfect cadence?
lookingFor: Clear grasp of basic harmonic vocabulary and its function, not just a rote definition.

bullets: State that a perfect cadence is V to I, giving a sense of resolution
State that an imperfect cadence ends on V, sounding unresolved or open
Give a musical example or describe the effect in a piece
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A perfect cadence moves from the dominant chord to the tonic, so V to I, and it's the strongest way to end a phrase because it resolves all the harmonic tension back home. An imperfect cadence ends on the dominant instead, so it sounds unfinished, like a question rather than a full stop. You hear that a lot at the end of the first half of a phrase in a hymn, where it leaves you expecting more music to follow.

commonMistakes: Confusing perfect and imperfect cadences
Reciting the definition with no sense of the musical effect
Not being able to give an example when asked
followUps: What about a plagal cadence, where does that fit in?

subtopic: Circle of fifths and key relationships
question: What is the circle of fifths, and why is it useful?
lookingFor: Solid theoretical understanding connected to practical musicianship, like modulation or key signatures.

bullets: Explain it maps keys by ascending or descending fifths, showing shared key signatures
Connect it to practical use, such as modulation or understanding closely related keys
Give a concrete example from repertoire or their own playing
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The circle of fifths arranges all twelve keys so that moving clockwise goes up a fifth each time, and adjacent keys on the circle share almost all the same notes in their key signature, differing by just one sharp or flat. It's useful because closely related keys, the ones next to each other on the circle, are the ones composers usually modulate into, so it helps me predict where a piece might be heading harmonically. When I'm sight-reading and I see a key change, I use the circle to quickly work out what's likely to have changed in the key signature.

commonMistakes: Being able to recite it but not explain why it matters
Confusing the order of sharps and flats
No connection to actual musical use
followUps: How would you use it to figure out a relative minor key?

question: Why do we tend to hear major keys as happy and minor keys as sad? Do you think that's always true?
lookingFor: Basic understanding of why the effect exists plus critical thinking about its limits.

bullets: Explain the interval difference, a minor third versus a major third, driving the perceived effect
Acknowledge it's a cultural convention as much as an acoustic fact
Give a counter-example where the rule doesn't hold
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It mostly comes down to the third of the scale, a minor third sits closer together and creates more tension against the root, which we've culturally learned to associate with sadness, while a major third sounds more open and settled. But I don't think it's a fixed rule. Plenty of minor key music is defiant or even joyful, like a lot of Klezmer music, and some major key pieces feel unsettling, like the end of Mahler's Sixth Symphony which is technically major but bleak. It's really more about how the harmony and orchestration are handled than the mode alone.

commonMistakes: Treating it as an absolute rule with no exceptions
No explanation of the actual interval difference
Confusing major and minor thirds
followUps: Can you think of a piece that breaks that expectation?

question: Can you walk us through the basic structure of sonata form?
lookingFor: A working grasp of a foundational large-scale form used across the classical repertoire.

bullets: Name the three main sections: exposition, development, recapitulation
Explain what happens in each, including theme and key relationships
Give an example from a piece they know
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Sonata form usually has three main parts. The exposition introduces a first theme in the tonic and a second theme in a contrasting key, often the dominant, with a bridge that gets you from one to the other. The development takes fragments of those themes and pushes them through different keys, which is usually the most harmonically unstable part of the movement. The recapitulation brings both themes back, but now both stay in the tonic key, which is what gives the movement its sense of resolution. I studied it closely in the first movement of Mozart's Symphony No. 40.

commonMistakes: Mixing up the order of the sections
Not knowing what actually happens in the development
No concrete example from real repertoire
followUps: Why might a composer choose to break from sonata form convention?

question: How would you go about identifying whether a chord you hear is major, minor, or diminished, without seeing the score?
lookingFor: Practical aural skill and a method for listening analytically, not just a claim of good ears.

bullets: Describe listening for the quality of the third and fifth above the root
Mention a practical method they actually use, such as singing intervals against a known reference
Show they've applied this in real playing or dictation, not just in theory
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I usually try to isolate the third first, because that's what tells you major or minor, a bright third sounds major and a darker, closer one sounds minor. Then I listen to the fifth, because if that sounds squashed rather than open, it's probably diminished. I trained this mostly through aural dictation at school and by testing myself on random chords on the piano with my eyes closed, which felt awkward at first but got much faster with practice. It's become second nature now when I'm learning a new piece by ear.

commonMistakes: No actual method, just claiming good ears
Confusing which interval signals major versus minor
Describing sight-reading instead of aural skills
followUps: How would that change for a seventh chord?

question: How do you approach sight-reading a piece you've never seen before?
lookingFor: A practical, disciplined method rather than just diving in and hoping for the best.

bullets: Describe scanning the piece first for key, time signature, and tricky spots
Explain prioritizing rhythm and overall shape over pausing for every wrong note
Show awareness that keeping going matters more than perfection
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Before I play a note I look through the piece for the key and time signature, and I scan for anything that jumps out, like awkward leaps or a sudden change of hand position. Then I try to feel the pulse before I start, usually counting a bar in silently, because losing the rhythm is what actually derails a sight-read, not a wrong note here or there. My rule for myself is to never stop and go back, even if I fumble something, because keeping the music moving matters more than getting every note right the first time.

commonMistakes: No pre-scan of the piece before starting
Stopping to fix every mistake instead of continuing
Prioritizing pitch accuracy over rhythm
followUps: What do you do when you completely lose your place?

question: Have you composed or arranged anything yourself? Tell us about it.
lookingFor: Genuine creative engagement with music-making, even at a modest level, described honestly.

bullets: Describe a specific piece or arrangement, however small, and what it was for
Explain a compositional choice they made and why
Reflect honestly on what they'd do differently now
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I arranged a folk song for string quartet for my sister's wedding, which was the first time I'd really had to think about voicing and register rather than just melody and chords. I decided to give the tune to the viola for the second verse instead of the violin, because I wanted a warmer color once the words turned more reflective. Looking back, my part-writing was a bit clumsy in places, there's some awkward parallel motion in the cello line, but it taught me more about how instruments actually sit together than any amount of listening had.

commonMistakes: Claiming composition experience with nothing concrete to show
No specific compositional decision explained
No honest reflection on weaknesses in the work
followUps: What would you compose next if you had free rein?

subtopic: A performance that changed their thinking
question: Tell us about a live performance you attended that changed how you think about music.
lookingFor: Genuine, reflective engagement with live music, showing how it shaped their musical thinking, not just a nice memory.

bullets: Name a specific performance and what actually happened musically
Explain what shifted in how they understood the music or performance
Connect it to how it influences their own playing or listening now
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I saw a string quartet perform Beethoven's Op. 132 and was struck by how differently the slow movement felt live compared to any recording I'd heard, the silences between phrases had weight I'd never noticed before. It made me realize how much interpretation lives in timing and space, not just notes on the page, which recordings tend to flatten out. Since then I've tried to be much more deliberate about silence in my own playing instead of treating rests as just gaps to get through.

commonMistakes: A generic 'it was amazing' with no musical detail
No real shift in thinking, just enthusiasm
Picking an event they clearly didn't engage with deeply
followUps: How has that changed the way you approach rests or pauses in your own playing?

question: Is a technically flawless performance always a better performance than one with a few mistakes but more feeling? What do you think makes a great performance?
lookingFor: Independent, well-reasoned musical judgment about the relationship between technique and expression.

bullets: Resist a simplistic answer either way, weighing both technique and expressive intent
Give a specific example supporting their view
Show understanding that technical security usually serves expression, not the reverse
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't think it's really a straight trade-off, because a lot of what we call feeling actually depends on technical control, phrasing and dynamic shading are technique too. But I'd still rather hear a performance with a couple of slips that's clearly communicating something than one that's note-perfect but emotionally flat, because the audience remembers the feeling far more than the accuracy. I think of pianists like Sviatoslav Richter, whose live recordings aren't always immaculate but are gripping, versus performances that are clean but forgettable. The goal isn't sloppiness, it's that technique should be in service of the music, not the other way around.

commonMistakes: Picking one extreme with no nuance
No concrete example to support the argument
Treating technique and expression as unrelated
followUps: Would your answer change for an audition versus a public concert?

question: What do you make of AI tools that can now generate music? Should musicians be worried?
lookingFor: Thoughtful, current engagement with a live issue in the field, avoiding both dismissal and panic.

bullets: Show awareness of what AI music tools can and can't currently do well
Weigh genuine concerns like labor and copyright against opportunities like composing aids
Land on a considered personal view, not just a shrug
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think it's worth taking seriously rather than dismissing. Some of these tools can generate competent background music very quickly, and that's a real threat to session and library music work in particular. But I don't think it replaces the kind of music-making I care about, where interpretation, live risk, and a performer's relationship with an audience are the point, not just the output of notes. I'm more interested in how composers might use these tools as a kind of sketching aid, the way photography changed painting rather than ended it. I do think the industry needs to get serious about consent and copyright for the material these models are trained on.

commonMistakes: Dismissing the topic entirely with no real engagement
Pure alarmism with no nuance
Not knowing basic facts about what current tools can do
followUps: Where do you think the line is between using a tool and losing authorship?

question: Classical music audiences are ageing and shrinking in many countries. How would you address that?
lookingFor: Realistic, informed engagement with a genuine structural issue facing the field, with concrete ideas.

bullets: Acknowledge the issue honestly rather than denying or minimizing it
Offer specific, realistic ideas around programming, venues, or access
Show awareness this isn't unique to classical music, or note counterexamples
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It's a real problem and I don't think pretending otherwise helps. Some of it is about programming, orchestras that only play the same fifteen warhorses aren't giving anyone a reason to come back, while ensembles that pair new commissions with standard repertoire, or perform in unconventional venues like warehouses or pubs, seem to be reaching younger audiences. Ticket price and the formality of concert etiquette matter too, a lot of people I know assume they'll do something wrong by clapping at the wrong moment and just don't go. I think the answer isn't dumbing anything down, it's removing the unnecessary barriers around access while keeping the music itself as ambitious as ever.

commonMistakes: Denying the problem exists
Vague calls to 'make it more accessible' with no specifics
Assuming the solution is simplifying the music itself
followUps: Do you think streaming has helped or hurt classical music specifically?

question: What have you been listening to recently outside your main area of focus?
lookingFor: Genuine curiosity and range beyond their comfort zone, not a performative list.

bullets: Name something specific and recent, not a vague genre
Explain what drew them to it or what they noticed
Show it's actually influenced their thinking, even in a small way
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've been listening to a lot of Ethiopian jazz recently, especially Mulatu Astatke, after a friend played me some on a long drive. What struck me was how the modal scales create a completely different harmonic feel from the Western jazz I know, it's not really major or minor in the way I'm used to thinking about it. It's pushed me to go back and question some of the assumptions I had about scale and mode being fixed categories, which has actually fed into how I've been improvising on my own instrument.

commonMistakes: A vague, generic answer like 'a bit of everything'
Naming something clearly said to impress rather than genuinely explored
No reflection on what it actually taught them
followUps: Did it change how you approach your main instrument at all?

question: Is there a period of music history you find particularly compelling? Why?
lookingFor: Genuine historical curiosity backed by specific composers, works, or context, not just a memorized label.

bullets: Name a specific period and what characterizes it musically
Explain what personally draws them to it, with named works or composers
Show some understanding of its historical or cultural context
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'm drawn to the early twentieth century, the period right around the First World War when composers like Stravinsky and Bartok were breaking away from tonal convention while folk music was becoming a serious compositional source rather than something to just quote decoratively. The Rite of Spring is the obvious example, but I find Bartok's string quartets even more interesting because you can watch him fuse Hungarian folk rhythms with a genuinely modern harmonic language across the six of them. It fascinates me because it's a period where composers were actively rebuilding what music could even be, right as the world around them was falling apart.

commonMistakes: Naming a period with no specific composers or works
Reciting textbook facts with no personal engagement
Getting basic chronology or context wrong
followUps: What do you think was lost, if anything, when tonality broke down?

question: What have you learned from playing chamber music or in an ensemble that you couldn't learn practicing alone?
lookingFor: Real insight into collaborative musicianship, not just teamwork platitudes.

bullets: Describe a specific ensemble experience, such as a quartet, band, choir, or orchestra
Explain a concrete skill that only comes from playing with others, like balance or non-verbal communication
Give an example of a moment this mattered in practice or performance
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Playing second violin in a string quartet taught me how much listening actually shapes a good ensemble sound, because my job is often to support the first violin's line rather than project my own, and figuring out exactly how much to pull back took real trial and error. There's also a kind of non-verbal communication you develop, a breath before an entrance, eye contact before a tempo change, that you simply can't practice on your own. During a performance once our cellist's string slipped out of tune mid-piece, and we adjusted our intonation around her in real time without anyone saying a word, which only happens because you've built that shared listening over months of rehearsal.

commonMistakes: Generic 'teamwork is important' with no specifics
Describing solo practice instead of actual ensemble interaction
No concrete example of a moment it mattered
followUps: How do you handle it when you disagree with another player's interpretation?

question: How do you deal with nerves before a performance or audition?
lookingFor: Honest, practical self-management strategies, not a claim of never being nervous.

bullets: Acknowledge nerves honestly rather than denying them
Describe a specific, concrete strategy they actually use
Show they've reflected on what works and what doesn't for them
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I still get nervous before every performance, and I've stopped trying to make that go away because I think a bit of adrenaline actually sharpens my playing. What I focus on instead is preparation, if I've run a piece enough times that my hands know it even when my mind goes blank, the nerves matter much less. I also do a short physical routine beforehand, slow breathing and shaking out my hands and shoulders, because I noticed tension in my arms was affecting my bow control more than the nerves themselves were.

commonMistakes: Claiming to never feel nervous
No concrete strategy, just vague reassurance
Describing avoidance rather than actual management
followUps: Has there been a time your preparation still wasn't enough? What happened?

question: Tell us about a time a teacher or conductor gave you tough feedback. How did you respond?
lookingFor: Maturity in receiving criticism and evidence of actually changing their playing because of it.

bullets: Describe genuinely difficult feedback, not a softened version
Show how they processed it without becoming defensive
Explain the concrete change it led to in their playing
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My conductor once told the whole section, in front of everyone, that our entrance in a Brahms symphony sounded timid and unconvincing, and it stung because I'd been the one leading that entrance. My first reaction was defensive, but once I actually listened back to a recording I realized she was right, I'd been so worried about accuracy that I'd stopped committing to the phrase. I spent the next week practicing that entrance louder and more confidently than felt comfortable, even risking a few wrong notes, and by the concert it had completely changed how it sounded.

commonMistakes: Picking feedback that wasn't actually hard to hear
Sounding defensive or blaming the teacher
No real change described afterward
followUps: How do you tell the difference between feedback worth acting on and feedback that's just one person's taste?

question: Have you used any music technology, like notation software or a DAW, in your work?
lookingFor: Practical familiarity with tools relevant to modern musicianship, described concretely.

bullets: Name specific software used and what they used it for
Describe a concrete project or task, not just familiarity in the abstract
Show understanding of what the tool is good and not good for
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I use MuseScore to notate my own arrangements because it's free and good enough for what I need, and I recently started experimenting with a basic DAW to record layered vocal harmonies for a small a cappella group I'm part of. It's useful for hearing back a rough mockup of an arrangement before rehearsal, which saves everyone time, but I've noticed the playback never quite tells you how a real ensemble will actually balance, so I still treat it as a sketch tool rather than a substitute for hearing it live.

commonMistakes: Vague claim of being 'good with technology' with no specifics
No actual project described
Overstating the role of software versus real musicianship
followUps: Do you think notation software changes how people compose?

subtopic: Contribution to the music community here
question: What would you bring to the ensembles and music community here beyond your own playing?
lookingFor: Evidence of genuine community-mindedness in music, not just self-promotion.

bullets: Point to a specific role they've played in a musical community before, such as organizing or mentoring
Connect it to something concrete they'd offer here, like a cross-genre collaboration idea
Avoid overpromising things outside their control
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: At school I organized a lunchtime chamber music series because I noticed a lot of good players never had anywhere informal to perform, and by the end of the year we had a rotating group of about twenty students taking part. I'd want to do something similar here, maybe cross-genre collaborations between the classical ensembles and the jazz society, since I've noticed those two worlds rarely mix even though a lot of players cross over. Mostly I just want to keep showing up and playing with as many different people as I can, because that's usually where I learn the most.

commonMistakes: Only talking about their own playing with no community angle
Overpromising leadership roles they can't guarantee
Vague enthusiasm with no concrete example from their past
followUps: What's stopped you from doing something like that already?

question: Do you see yourself pursuing music as a performing career, or does this degree serve a different purpose for you?
lookingFor: Honest, realistic reflection on their relationship to music as a possible career, without needing a fixed answer.

bullets: Give an honest current view, acknowledging uncertainty is normal at this stage
Show they understand the range of paths a music degree can lead to, beyond just performing
Connect the answer back to why this particular degree still makes sense for them
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Honestly, I'm not certain I want to be a full-time performer, the odds are tough and I want to make that decision with clear eyes rather than out of naivety. What I am certain of is that I want music to be central to whatever I do, whether that's performing, arts administration, or even music therapy, which I became interested in after volunteering at a care home. This degree appeals to me precisely because it doesn't force that choice yet, it lets me keep performing seriously while also studying the wider field, so I can make a more informed decision by the time I graduate.

commonMistakes: Pretending total certainty about a performing career with no realism
Sounding like they don't actually want to keep playing seriously
Not connecting the answer back to why this course fits
followUps: What would make you confident enough to commit to a performing career?
